title: In These Fields of My Own Land...
text:
In these fields of my own land
and a stranger in the fields of my country
—I had a homeland where the Duero runs
among gray crags,
and ghosts of ancient holm-oak groves,
there in Castile, mystical and warlike,
Castile the gentle, humble and bold,
Castile of disdain and strength—,
in these fields of my Andalusia,
oh land where I was born! I would like to sing.
I have memories of my childhood, I have
images of light and palm trees,
and in a glory of gold,
of far-off bell towers with storks,
of cities with streets without women
beneath an indigo sky, deserted squares
where blazing orange trees grow
with their round, crimson fruits;
and in a shadowy orchard, the lemon tree
with dusty branches
and pale yellow lemons,
which the clear water of the fountain reflects,
a scent of tuberoses and carnations
and a strong smell of basil and spearmint;
images of gray olive groves
beneath a scorching sun that stuns and blinds,
and blue, scattered mountain ranges
with the afterglows of an immense afternoon;
but the thread that memory ties
to the heart is missing, the anchor at its bank,
or these memories have no soul. They bear
in their motley garments
the sign of being the remnants of memory,
the brute burden memory carries.
One day they will return, anointed with light from the depths,
the virginal bodies to the old shore.
editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish rendering. The source opens with the syntactically unusual pair ‘En estos campos... / y extranjero...’; that ambiguity and the source lineation are retained. The split OCR form ‘d-el fondo’ is rendered as ‘from the depths,’ and minor punctuation spacing was normalized.

title: April Was Blooming
text:
April was blooming
before my window.
Among the jasmine
and the white roses
of a flower-filled balcony,
I saw the two sisters.
The younger sewed,
the elder spun …
Among the jasmine
and the white roses,
the littlest one,
laughing and rosy,
her needle in the air?,
looked toward my window.


The elder went on,
silent and pale,
the spindle on her distaff
coiling the linen.
April was blooming
before my window.


One clear afternoon
the elder was weeping,
among the jasmine
and the white roses,
and before the white linen
she spun on her distaff.
What is wrong? I said to her.
Silent, pale,
she pointed to the dress
the sister had begun.
On the black tunic
the needle gleamed;
over the white veil,
the silver thimble.
She pointed to the April
afternoon that dreamed,
while the ringing of bells
could be heard.
And in the clear afternoon
she showed me her tears…
April was blooming
before my window.


It was another joyful April
and another peaceful afternoon.
The flower-filled balcony
was solitary…
Neither the littlest one,
laughing and rosy,
nor the sad sister,
silent and pale,
nor the black tunic,
nor the white coif…
Only on the spindle
the linen turned
by an invisible hand,
and in the dark room
the moon in the clean
mirror shone…
Among the jasmine
and the white roses
of the flower-filled balcony,
I looked at myself in the clear
moon of the mirror
that dreamed far away…
April was blooming
before my window.
editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish rendering. The source body lacks the opening phrase supplied by the catalog title and begins with ‘frente a mi ventana’; ‘April was blooming’ has been restored as the first line, matching the later refrain, and this restoration is explicit here. Source stanza breaks and ellipses are retained.

title: Of the Ephemeral Past
text:
This man from the provincial casino
        who saw Carancha take the charge one day,
        has a withered complexion, hair gone gray,
        eyes veiled in melancholy;
        beneath the gray mustache, lips of weariness,
        and a sad expression that is not sadness,
        but something more and less: the emptiness
        of the world in the hollow of his head.


        He still wears purple velvet,
        a jacket and trousers tapered to his shoes,
        and a caramel-colored Cordoban hat,
        polished and turned.
        Three times he inherited; three times at monte
        he lost his fortune; twice he was widowed.


        He comes alive only before forbidden chance,
        reclining over the green baize,
        or when recalling a bullfighter's afternoon,
        a gambler's luck, or when someone recounts
        the exploit of a gallant bandit,
        or the bloody feat of a tough.


        He yawns out banal political
        insults at the reactionary government,
        and predicts that the liberals will come,
        as the stork returns to the belfry.


        A bit of a farmer, he waits for the sky
        and fears the sky; sometimes he sighs,
        thinking of his olive grove, and looks at the sky
        with an anxious eye when the rain is late.


        Everything else, taciturn, hypochondriacal,
        prisoner in the Arcadia of the present,
        bores him; only tobacco smoke
        simulates a few shadows on his brow.


        This man is neither of yesterday nor tomorrow,
        but of never; from the Hispanic stock
        he is neither the ripe nor the rotten fruit,
        but a barren fruit
        of that Spain which passed and never was,
        that Spain whose head is gray today.
editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish rendering. The source's indented verse layout and stanza breaks are retained; ‘Carancha’ and ‘monte’ are preserved as bullfighting and gambling references. ‘Abotinado’ is rendered as trousers tapered to the shoes, and ‘un poco labrador’ as ‘a bit of a farmer’ to restore the idioms.

title: My Childhood Is Memories of a Courtyard in Seville...
text:
My childhood is memories of a courtyard in Seville,

a bright orchard where the lemon tree ripens;

my youth, twenty years in the lands of Castile;

my story, a few things I would rather not recall.


Neither a seducer Mañara nor a Bradomín have I been

—you know my clumsy way of dressing—,

but I received the arrow Cupid assigned me,

and I loved whatever they might have that was hospitable.


There are drops of Jacobin blood in my veins,

but my verse springs from a tranquil source;

and, more than a conventional man who knows his doctrine,

I am, in the good sense of the word, good.


I adore beauty, and in modern aesthetics

I cut the old roses from Ronsard's garden;

but I do not love the cosmetics of today's fashion,

nor am I one of those birds of the new gay singing.


I disdain the romances of hollow tenors

and the chorus of crickets that sing to the moon.

I stop to distinguish voices from echoes,

and among the voices I listen to only one.


Am I classical or romantic? I do not know. I would like to leave

my verse as a captain leaves his sword:

famous for the virile hand that wielded it,

not prized for the learned craft of its forger.


I converse with the man who always goes with me

—he who speaks alone hopes to speak to God one day—;

my soliloquy is a conversation with that good friend

who taught me the secret of philanthropy.


And in the end, I owe you nothing; you owe me all I have written.

I go to my work, and with my money I pay for

the clothes that cover me and the house I inhabit,

the bread that feeds me and the bed where I lie.


And when the day of the final journey arrives,

and the ship that will never return is about to depart,

you will find me aboard, light of baggage,

almost naked, like the children of the sea.
editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish rendering. The poem's repeated blank lines, parenthetical dashes, and final nautical image are preserved.

title: The Stolen Heart
text:
My sad heart drools astern,
my heart the corporal fills
and pours streams of soup into it,
my sad heart drools astern:
with the troop's bloody jokes
that roar a general guffaw,
my sad heart drools astern,
my heart the corporal fills!


Ithyphallic and soldierly,
their bloody jokes have corrupted it;
and at night they paint some frescoes,
ithyphallic and soldierly.
O abracadabrant waves,
carry my heart away, let it be washed!
Ithyphallic and soldierly,
their bloody jokes have corrupted it.


When their gargalic chimos run out,
how shall I live, O stolen heart?
their Bacchic refrains will arrive;
when their gargalic chimos run out
I will feel stomachic jolts,
I, he of the shattered heart.
When their gargalic chimos run out,
how shall I live, O stolen heart?
editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish rendering, rather than from Rimbaud's French original. The deliberately grotesque refrain and opaque terms ‘gargalic chimos’ are retained as rendered; stanza and refrain structure are preserved.

title: The Crows
text:
Lord, when the meadows are cold
and when in the beaten-down villages
the very slow Angelus has fallen silent,
over the field stripped of its flowers
let the delightful crows fall from the sky,
so dear.


Strange host of cries of justice,
the north wind has entered your nests!
On the banks of yellow rivers,
by the path of the old calvaries,
and at the bottom of the pit and the grave,
disperse yourselves, unite.


By the thousands, over the fields of France,
where our dead of old sleep,
turn and turn, in winter,
so that the traveler, passing, will remember.
Be heralds of duty, O our
black funeral birds!


Saints of heaven, atop the oak,
mast lost in the enchanted night,
leave the spring warbler
for him who in the forest binds,
beneath the grass that bars escape,
the disastrous defeat.
editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish rendering, rather than from Rimbaud's French original. The address to the crows, imperative movement, and stanza structure are preserved; the source's doubled exclamation was regularized.

title: First Evening
text:
Naked, almost naked;
and the gossiping trees
pressed up to the window,
rascals, their rascal foliage.


Seated in my armchair,
naked, she clasped her hands.
And on the floor, her little feet
trembled with delight.


—I saw how, wax-colored,
a ray with the light of foliage
fluttered over her laughter
and her breast—a fly on a flower,


—I kissed her delicate ankles.
And she burst into laughter, so soft,


beautiful crystal laughter,
scattered in clear trills…


Beneath the chemise, her feet
—‘Enough, enough!’—hid themselves.
—Laughter, false punishment
for the first boldness!


Trembling, poor, her eyes
my lips kissed, softly:
—She tossed her head back, coyly: ‘Better, if you can…!


Sir, two words…’—
She swallowed what remained
with a kiss that made her
laugh… how pleased she was!


—Naked, almost naked;
and the gossiping trees
peered in at the window,
rascals, their rascal foliage.
editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish rendering, rather than from Rimbaud's French original. The flirtatious dialogue, repeated opening/closing stanza, and source stanza breaks are preserved; mismatched quotation marks and minor punctuation spacing were normalized.

title: The Lice-Pickers
text:
When the infant forehead, with its red storms,
calls up the white swarm of vague dreams,
two laughing sisters come to the bedside
with their graceful fingers, silver-nailed.


They seat the child before the open window,
where blue air bathes whirlwinds of flowers,
and through his thick hair, heavy with dew,
their fingers pass, seductive, terrible.


He listens to the song of their timid breaths,
which spread broad honeys of plants and roses
and are sometimes interrupted by a whistle—saliva
the lips draw in, or the desire to kiss.


He hears their eyelashes beat in the perfumed
silence; and their fingers, electric and soft,
bring about, amid gray indolences, the clicks
of dead lice crushed by their queenly nails.


And a wine of Sloth rises in him, a harmonica
sigh capable of reaching delirium:
and the child feels, to the slow rhythm of the caresses,
how his urges to weep are born and die.
editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish rendering, rather than from Rimbaud's French original. The unsettling tenderness, bodily ambiguity, and stanza structure are preserved.

title: Parisian War Song
text:
Spring has arrived:
from the depths of the green Estates,
the flight of Thiers and Picard,
unfurled, weaves its splendor.


Naked asses, mad! May!
Listen, then, how Sèvres, Meudon,
Bagneux and Asnières sow us
these flowers of spring.


They have shako, saber and tantan;
they left the old lanterns behind;
and canoes that chug… chug… chug…
traverse the lakes with blood.


We are more on a spree than ever
when through our burrows
the blond cabochons fall
that light secret dawns.


Thiers and Picard are Eroses,
raptors of heliotropes
who paint Corots with bombs:
their tropes come buzzing now


Favre, lying among gladioli,
blinks like an aqueduct


with peppery groans…
They are pals of the Great Trick!


The great city burns, despite
your showers of petroleum:
you will have to leave
for another episode to begin…


And the Rural Guards who doze,
crouching, day and night,
will hear the branches as they break,
moved by reddish rustlings!
editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish rendering, rather than from Rimbaud's French original. Proper names, military vocabulary, obscene jolt, painterly references, and stanza breaks are retained; the source typo ‘vayais’ was rendered by its clear second-person plural sense.

title: Amaranth Flowerbeds Up To...
text:
Amaranth flowerbeds up to

the agreeable palace of Jupiter.

— I know it is You who, here,

mix Your Blue, almost Saharan!


Then, like roses and sunlit firs

and vines whose games are fenced in,

widow's cage…!


Singular

troops of birds, oh iao, iao…!


— Peaceful mansion, ancient passion!

Kiosk of the Madwoman by affection.

Behind rosebush bottoms, Juliet's

shadowy, very low balcony.


— Juliet reminds me of Henrietta,

that charming railway station

on a mountain, as at the back of an orchard

where a thousand blue devils can be seen dancing!


Green bench where panting paradise sings,

on the guitar, the pale Irishwoman.

Then in the dining room, Guianese-style,

chatter of cages and of some children.


Duke's window through which I think

of boxwood poison and of snails

sleeping here beneath the suns.

Excessive beauty! Let us keep silent.


— Boulevard without commerce or movement,

silent, all drama and all performance,

you are the gathering of infinite scenes,

I recognize and admire you in silence.
editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish rendering, rather than from Rimbaud's French original. The surreal syntax, capitalized ‘Blue,’ names, invented/opaque diction, and unusually spaced lineation are preserved; the source's singular ‘se duerme’ is kept as the deliberately ambiguous participle ‘sleeping.’

title: The Frightened Ones
text:
Black in the snow and mist,

before the great skylight that glows

with their bottoms in a ring,


kneeling, five hungry children

watch the baker make

a loaf of gold…


They see the strong white arm turn

in the gray dough being baked

in the bright mouth,


and hear the rich bread cooking;
and the baker, laughing happily,

sings his tune


They crowd before the red skylight,

still, to receive its breath

warm as a breast;


and when, at twelve, the bread comes out

polished, rounded and crisp,

of a dark golden blond,


when, beneath the smoked beams,

the fragrant crusts sing,

like the cricket sings,


when that hot mouth breathes

life… with a happy soul

sheltered in rags,


they realize how well they live…

Poor children dressed by frost!

—All huddled together,


pressing their pink little muzzles

to the bars; they sing anything

through the openings,


softly, softly—like a prayer…

leaning toward the clear light

of this new heaven,


so tense that their trousers burst:

and their white poor people's shirts

tremble in the north wind.
editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish rendering, rather than from Rimbaud's French original. The children’s repeated visual focus on the bakery window, the source’s short-line stanza pattern, and its ironic warmth are preserved; the source's collective singular ‘alma’ remains singular in ‘a happy soul.’

title: Tomorrow
text:
Was I not once possessed of a gentle, heroic, fabulous youth, worthy of being written on golden leaves?—Too much luck! By what crime, by what error, have I deserved my present weakness? You who maintain that beasts sob with sorrow, that the sick despair, that the dead have nightmares, try to relate my torpor and my fall. For as for me, I can no longer express myself except like the beggar with his continual
Pater
and
Ave Maria
. I no longer even know how to speak!


Nevertheless, today at last, I believe I have finished the account of my hell. It was surely hell; the ancient one, the one where the son of man opened the doors.


From the same desert, in the same night, my tired eyes always awaken to the silver star, without the Kings of life being moved—the three magi, the heart, the soul, the spirit. When shall we go, beyond the shores and mountains, to greet the birth of the new work, of the new wisdom, the flight from tyrants and demons, the end of superstition, to adore—the first!—Christmas upon the earth?


The song of the heavens, the march of peoples! Slaves, let us not curse life.




A Season in Hell
, 1873
editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish rendering, rather than from Rimbaud's French original. The prose paragraphs, standalone Pater/Ave Maria lines, rhetorical questions, and closing work/date attribution are preserved.

title: My Little Loves
text:
A tearful hydrolith washes

the cabbage-colored skies

beneath the tree of tender shoots

that your rubbers drool,


white, with their singular moons

and their round pialatos:

clash your kneecaps

my beloved monstrosities!


In those days we loved one another,

my blue and sad monstrosity!

we ate eggs by the minute

and sky-colored chickweed.


One night you anointed me a poet,

my blond, blue-eyed monstrosity:

come to my side, I want to whip you

when you are in my lap.


I vomited your fat bandoline,

glossy black monstrosity:

you, my big bandoneon, would cut me

clean, level with the hair.


How disgusting, my dried saliva,

red-haired monstrosity,

still poisons the trenches

of your two ample breasts!


My little loves,

how very, very much I can hate you!

Patch up with sad slaps

your disgusting tits!


Jump, jump, old bowls

full of feeling;

come on, jump, become dancers

for just a moment!


Your shoulder blades come unjointed,

loves, my loves:

with a star on your backs, lame,

keep on with your turns!


And to top it all, I have rhymed

in honor of these haunches!

If only I could break your hips

and redeem myself from my love!


Grace-less heap of broken stars,

return to your corners—

You will burst in God, your panniers well loaded

with disgrace.

Under the particular moons

and their round pialatos,

clash your kneecaps,

my beloved monstrosities!
editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish rendering, rather than from Rimbaud's French original. The poem’s abusive grotesquerie, invented terms (‘hydrolith,’ ‘pialatos’), sexual imagery, repeated refrain, and stanza spacing are preserved.

title: Adventure
text:
I


At seventeen, you cannot be serious.

—One evening, you grow sick of pitchers and lemonade,

of noisy cafés with dazzling polish!

—And you go off among the green linden trees of the avenue.


How wonderfully the lindens smell on June evenings!

The air is so soft that you must lower your eyelids;

And the murmuring wind—the city is not far away—

brings scents of vines and scents of beer.


II


Suddenly one can see in the sky a scrap

of sea-blue, framed by the branch of a little tree,

and pierced, fatally, by a star, while it melts

with very sweet tremors, tiny and so white…


Seventeen! June night!—You get drunk.

The sap is champagne rising to your head…

You drift; and sense on your lips a kiss

that throbs in the mouth, like a little animal.


 III


Madly, your soul plays Robinson in novels,

—when, in the brightness of a pale streetlamp,

a young lady of charming appearance passes,

in the shadow of her father's horrible neck.


And since she thinks you immensely naive,

as her boots trot along the pavements,

she turns, alert, and with an expressive gesture…

—And on your lips, then, a cavatina dies…


   IV


You are in love. Rented until August.

You are in love. She laughs at your verses.

Your friends leave; you are unbearable.

—And one evening, your sweetheart deigns at last to write to you…!


And that evening… you return to the bright café,

ask again for pitchers full of lemonade…

—At seventeen, you cannot be serious,

when the green lindens crown the avenue.
editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish rendering, rather than from Rimbaud's French original. The four-part structure, direct second-person address, ellipses, and source’s playful shifts in register are preserved; minor dash spacing was normalized.

title: The Lightning
text:
Human work is the explosion that lights my abyss from time to time!


‘Nothing is vanity; onward toward science, and forward!’ cries the modern Ecclesiastes, which is to say Everyone. And yet the corpses of the wicked and the idle fall upon the hearts of others… Ah, quickly, a little faster! There, beyond the night, those future, eternal rewards… will we be able to evade them…?


—What can I do? I know work; and science is too slow. Let prayer gallop and let light thunder… that seems fine to me. It is too simple, and it is too hot; surely they will continue without me. I have my duty, and I will take pride in it in the same way as many do, by setting it aside.


My life is spent. Come! Let us pretend, let us wander, O pity! And we shall exist by amusing ourselves, dreaming of monstrous loves and fantastic universes, complaining and demanding the world's appearances, acrobat, beggar, artist, bandit—priest! In my hospital bed, the intense smell of incense has enveloped me again; guardian of sacred aromas, confessor, martyr…


I recognize in this the filthy education of my childhood. So what!… To live my twenty years because others live their twenty years…


No! No! From now on I rebel against death! Work seems too light to my pride: my betrayal of the world would be too short a torment. At the last moment, I would strike right and left…


Then—oh, poor beloved soul!—perhaps we have not yet lost eternity!




A Season in Hell
, 1873
editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish rendering, rather than from Rimbaud's French original. The prose paragraphing, abrupt apostrophes, em dashes, and closing work/date attribution are preserved.
